problems.memo_sentence: The paper studies variational quantum optimisation for combinatorial problems mapped to QUBO, including Max-Cut, number partitioning, and NP-complete portfolio optimisation, the latter being the core finance application considered.
problems.source_evidence: “We test our proposed objective function, in an emulation environment, using as case-studies three different optimisation problems: Max-Cut, Number Partitioning and Portfolio Optimisation.” ... “Portfolio optimisation as given in Eq. (14) was recently tackled using variational quantum algorithms...”
problems.explanation: The memo presents portfolio optimisation as the core finance application, but the paper treats it as one of three equal case studies. The source does not single it out as the core application.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors emphasize using hybrid quantum-classical algorithms in the NISQ era and focus on how measurement outcomes are used to define the objective function rather than on changing the ansatz or measurement scheme.
problems.source_evidence: “What we focus in this contribution is the third part, and specifically on how to use the measurement outcomes performed in estimating the energy of a quantum state to (i) accelerate the speed and (ii) improve the accuracy...”
problems.explanation: The paper does focus on the objective function, but the memo adds a stronger contrast with ansatz/measurement-scheme changes that is not explicitly made in the source. This is a mild overstatement of emphasis.

problems.memo_sentence: The method varies the CVaR tail parameter α during optimisation using predefined linear or sigmoid schedules, optionally truncating the evolution before α reaches 1 and scaling the number of shots as K/α, with evaluations carried out on the Qiskit Aer simulator using COBYLA for all problem instances and using overlap with the optimal solution as the primary metric with a 10% success threshold.
problems.source_evidence: “We ran our experiments on IBM’s Qiskit Aer simulator...” ... “We used the same gradient-free optimiser, COBYLA, for all different problems and instances...” ... “The second metric we want to test is the time taken to reach a given fixed overlap. We set a threshold of 10% probability...”
problems.explanation: The memo omits that the paper also evaluates approximation ratio and normalized optimizer iterations, and that the 10% threshold is only one of several metrics. It also compresses the discussion of truncating at ε into a general method description without the paper’s framing that this is optional and problem-dependent.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper studies variational quantum optimisation for combinatorial problems mapped to QUBO, including Max-Cut, number partitioning, and NP-complete portfolio optimisation, the latter being the core finance application considered.
problems.source_evidence: “We test our proposed objective function, in an emulation environment...”
problems.explanation: The source explicitly states the experiments are performed in an emulation environment, which is an important limitation of the study. The memo does not reflect this anywhere in its problem framing.

problems.memo_sentence: The work proposes Ascending-CVaR, an evolving objective function for VQE/QAOA that starts from a CVaR-style tail objective and gradually approaches the full energy expectation, inspired by prior tail-based objectives and adiabatic quantum computing.
problems.source_evidence: “However, knowing the maximum overlap κ in advance is not always possible.” ... “In the case of VQE with a hardware eﬃcient ansatz, it can be shown that κ = 1 ... On the other hand for the QAOA ansatz, our experiments showed that κ is usually small on low depth but increases with the number of layers”
problems.explanation: The paper explicitly notes that the key overlap threshold κ is not generally known in advance and behaves differently for VQE and QAOA. The memo presents the method more cleanly than the paper allows, without reflecting this limitation.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors also report that VQE with Ascending-CVaR consistently outperforms QAOA in these tests, that Ascending-CVaR can erase spurious local minima as α increases, and that on easy regular Max-Cut instances all objectives perform similarly while improvements are more pronounced on harder, irregular instances.
problems.source_evidence: “We note that for all three combinatorial optimisation problems and for all methods used ... VQE performs (much) better than QAOA, at least for the sufficiently shallow circuits that we consider.” ... “In the QAOA algorithm we tested instances using depth p = 1 to p = 6 while on VQE we worked only on the depth p = 1...”
problems.explanation: The memo states the VQE-vs-QAOA comparison as a broad result, but the paper’s conclusion is limited to the shallow depths tested. That limitation materially qualifies the claim.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper claims novelty in introducing an evolving, Ascending-CVaR objective function for variational quantum optimisation that starts from a CVaR tail and gradually becomes the full energy expectation, inspired by adiabatic quantum computing, and in formally analysing how changing α preserves the global minimum while potentially removing local minima.
problems.source_evidence: “As it was proven by [11], the angles θ∗ that minimise CVaRα do not (in general) correspond to minima of the expectation value.” ... “Proposition 1. ...” ... “Proposition 3 was proven using a counterexample in [11].”
problems.explanation: The paper’s formal statements about CVaR minima and local minima are partly attributed to Barkoutsos et al. [11], not newly proved here. The memo attributes the formal analysis to this paper without distinguishing what is inherited from the cited reference.

problems.source_evidence: Results section: “For all three combinatorial optimisation problems and for all methods used ... VQE performs (much) better than QAOA...” and “CVaRαt-QAOA ... underperforms significantly...”
problems.explanation: The memo foregrounds the benchmark problems and finance framing, but it underplays the paper’s substantive results section, especially the repeated finding that QAOA performs poorly relative to VQE. This is a mild section-bias issue.
